detail.abstract: Price stability is an indispensable foundation of macroeconomic stability, but it cannot by itself ensure economic sustainability, meaning the economy’s underlying capacity to absorb shocks and return to a stable trajectory. This paper argues that inequality is not merely a distributional outcome but a structural condition that shapes aggregate demand, balance-sheet resilience, expectations, and the transmission of monetary policy. The paper proceeds in three steps. First, it identifies three mutually reinforcing preconditions for economic sustainability: effective distributional and resource-allocation mechanisms, sound balance sheets, and institutional legitimacy. It shows how technological change, globalization, financialization, and lagging institutional frameworks have eroded them. Second, it shows how the erosion of these preconditions has changed the environment through which monetary policy operates, shifting the composition of monetary transmission rather than simply weakening it. Effects through broad-based employment income, consumption, and productive investment have become less reliable relative to effects through asset prices, collateral values, and credit conditions, and they are increasingly asymmetric between easing and tightening. Third, it shows how this changing composition of monetary transmission interacts with existing inequality and financial vulnerabilities to create a self-reinforcing macro-financial feedback loop, giving inequality the character of a system-level risk even where price stability is maintained. The paper does not call for expanding central-bank mandates. Instead, it argues that central banks should incorporate distributional and balance-sheet heterogeneity into monetary-policy and financial-stability analysis. This should be supported by shared diagnostics and coordinated action across governments, regulators, and market actors within their respective responsibilities.

detail.abstract: Youn and Chatterjea (2025) modelled cognitive control as a stochastic differential game between prefrontal (PFC) and limbic populations, and a later extension added fractional noise and jumps. Two issues limit that theory. First, long-memory noise makes the state non-Markovian, so Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs (HJI) value functions of (t, x) are not well defined. Second, Nash equilibrium presupposes perfectly rational, noise-free policies, and control failure, the event that matters clinically, is studied only by simulation. We make three contributions. (i) We replace fractional Brownian forcing by a finite-dimensional Markovian lift, a weighted sum of Ornstein-Uhlenbeck factors with power-law weights, and prove an L 2 error bound in terms of the kernel approximation error. (ii) We replace Nash equilibrium by an entropy-regularised (quantalresponse) equilibrium with bounded controls. We show that the equilibrium policies are Gibbs measures with feedback Lipschitz constants uniform in the rationality temperature, prove existence and uniqueness within the class of Lipschitz-regular equilibria, obtain an explicit O(√ τ) convergence to the classical Nash value, and show that the equilibrium of the lifted game is a δ-Nash equilibrium of the exact long-memory game. (iii) We model control failure as noise-induced escape from the PFC-dominant attractor of the lifted closed-loop system. Freidlin-Wentzell theory gives a Kramerstype escape law. In a reduced order-parameter model we sandwich the escape barrier between its uncontrolled and classical-Nash values, and we characterise the memory channel through a frequency-weighted large-deviation cost. We also record corrections to several statements in the earlier extension. All results are theoretical, and empirical validation on recorded data is left open.

detail.abstract:
Enterprise AI capability and enterprise financial return are different outcomes, and between 2025 and 2026 they visibly diverged. This paper, the third in a series, reviews 87 source records, most published in 2025 and 2026: randomized and quasi-experimental workplace studies, administrative-data studies, official statistics, large executive surveys, capability benchmarks and company disclosures. Each record is appraised separately for causal credibility and for proximity to net financial return, and no record in the review is strong on both.

Five findings emerge. First, measured capability compounded while reported value did not: the length of software tasks frontier models complete with 50% success rose from about one hour to about twelve hours between February 2025 and February 2026, and the best published expert-comparison win-or-tie rate rose from 48% to 85%, yet the share of organizations attributing any EBIT impact to AI was 39% in 2025 and 37% in 2026, with high performers flat near 6%. Second, task-level causal effects are real but heterogeneous, ranging from 15% to 26% throughput gains in customer support and software to null or adverse effects elsewhere, and population-level time savings remain near 2% of US work hours, with Danish administrative data ruling out earnings effects above 2%. Third, firms report little realized value: about nine in ten of some 6,000 firms report no productivity effect over three years (realized about 0.3%, expected 1.4%), and 56% of 4,454 CEOs report neither revenue nor cost benefit. Fourth, the cost side is poorly measured: unit prices at fixed capability fall roughly five- to tenfold a year while volumes and capital spending rise, review-inclusive gains on an expert benchmark fall from 90 times faster to 1.12 times, and no company disclosure examined reports AI benefit and full AI cost on the same defined scope with a stated counterfactual. Fifth, returns are concentrated, and the strongest positive firm-level causal estimate, about 4% higher labor productivity, is conditional on complementary investment.

The synthesis reframes the enterprise problem as one of conversion: capability is necessary and increasingly abundant, while value depends on workflow redesign, capacity capture and measurement. The paper revisits the earlier papers' claims, retains business-AI integration as a plausible organizational capability rather than a causally established role, and contributes an evidence map, a disclosure audit with a minimum disclosure standard for AI value claims, an evidence-gated decision framework, and a cluster-randomized design to test the integrator hypothesis.

detail.abstract: The growing use of AI as a source of information extends a longstanding pattern: different people may privately observe the same signal. I study how such shared private signals shape learning from others' choices. Repeated reliance on one signal can encourage herding, while the possibility of a shared source can make agents less willing to follow earlier choices against their independent information. When the shared signal is less accurate than independent signals, a sufficiently small share of users can improve learning under random tiebreaking, but a majority raises the probability of an incorrect herd relative to an economy with only independent agents. When the shared signal is more accurate, further accuracy gains can make its mistakes harder to correct and increase the probability of an incorrect herd. A sufficiently accurate shared signal determines the direction of herding. Neither making the shared signal public nor disclosing the information source behind each choice uniformly improves learning.

detail.abstract: Post-earnings-announcement drift (PEAD) is one of the most widely studied anomalies in empirical finance. In liquid, heavily arbitraged markets the effect has been competed away, weakening the strategy's returns. In the least liquid parts of the market, like micro- and small-cap equities, institutional capital is constrained leading to different market conditions that are less explored. This paper studies a long-only PEAD strategy in US micro-and small-capitalization equities from the period 2015 to 2024, using a price-reaction surprise proxy and using the QuantConnect default fee model for US equities. The strategy produces economically meaningful returns of 8.9% and 12.2% as well as positive risk-adjusted alpha net of fees across versions. The return attribution analysis isolates the earnings surprise signal from broader market exposure. To fix the strategy's structural susceptibility to cash drag, it sweeps non-deployed capital into Treasury Bills. Measuring the returns of the deployed portion alone, returns are 13.5% and 16.5% respectively across versions. The illiquid nature of the strategy leads to capacity limits, which are estimated to link to the constraints that sustain the anomaly and limit institutional capital. This study executes a friction-sensitive strategy that generates economically meaningful returns while reserving the 2025+ period for out-of-sample future verification.

detail.abstract:
The Lucas Paradox—the observation that capital does not systematically flow from capital-abundant to capital-scarce economies despite potentially higher returns in the latter—remains a fundamental puzzle in international economics. This paper develops a theory of Opportunity Realization Costs (ORC) to explain why economically attractive investment opportunities do not necessarily become productive investments.

The theory's central proposition is that international capital allocation depends not only on the potential returns to investment but also on the conditions governing its realization. It conceptualizes the conversion of an investment opportunity into a productive asset as a sequential process shaped by information acquisition, strategic interaction between foreign investors and host states, and structural constraints affecting capital mobilization and project development.

The theory identifies six dimensions of Opportunity Realization Costs and distinguishes five phases of investment realization, from opportunity recognition to sustained productive use. It explains how constraints across these dimensions and phases affect investment participation and the probability of successful realization. A formal framework integrates these relationships, derives theoretical propositions, and establishes an approach to empirical operationalization.

The paper advances a theoretical explanation rather than claiming empirical validation. Its central contribution is to shift the explanation of the Lucas Paradox from the geographical distribution of potential returns to the conditions under which investment opportunities become realizable. An investment opportunity is not an investable reality.

detail.abstract: Modern Anglo-American private-law theory remains divided over the ontological status of the constructive trust-specifically, whether it is a substantive property institution born of the historical split between law and equity in the English Court of Chancery, or a flexible remedial formula responding to unjust enrichment and unconscionability. The legal system of Pakistan offers an extraordinary comparative laboratory that unsettles both poles of this debate. Operating within a unitary property regime that expressly rejected dual legal and equitable estates in the nineteenth-century Anglo-Indian codes, Pakistani jurisprudence has forged a tri-layered normative architecture of fiduciary loyalty and constructive restitution. This Article provides the first comprehensive philosophical, jurisprudential, and pan-statutory account of constructive trusts and fiduciary relations in Pakistan from colonial codification to the present. First, at the level of legal philosophy, this Article traces how nineteenth-century Anglo-Indian codifiers synthesized Roman-Germanic civilian obligation theory-as mediated through John Austin, David Dudley Field's New York Civil Code drafts, and Robert Joseph Pothier-with English equity doctrines across the Contract Act of 1872, the Specific Relief Act of 1877, the Transfer of Property Act of 1882, and the Trusts Act of 1882. Second, it examines the postcolonial jurisprudential shift spearheaded by the superior courts of Pakistan in landmark decisions such as Haji Nizam Khan v. Additional District Judge, Lyallpur and Qazalbash Waqf v. Chief Land Commissioner, which decolonized the statutory residual clause of "justice, equity, and good conscience" and re-anchored uncodified equitable remedies in Islamic legal philosophy (Usul al-Fiqh)-specifically, the doctrines of Amanah (fiduciary stewardship), Istihsan (juristic equity), Maslahah Mursalah (unrestricted public interest), and the prohibition of Akl al-Mal bil-Batil (unjust enrichment).

detail.abstract:
Innovation-intensive start-ups can enrich competition, especially in concentrated markets. Yet acquisitions of such firms often escape the scrutiny of competition authorities, as turnover thresholds fail to capture targets that generate little or no revenue, which is often the case with start-ups. At the same time, it is these start-ups that are popular targets for incumbents. While empirical evidence of killer acquisitions remains inconclusive, related theories of harm (eg loss of potential competition and loss of innovation competition, including reverse killer acquisitions) attach to the same target profile.

Since the Illumina/Grail judgment took the Article 22 EUMR referral mechanism off the table for such cases, an enforcement gap remains despite transaction value thresholds, call-in powers in several Member States, Article 14 DMA and sector inquiries.

This paper proposes a novel target-based trigger: an information duty in German merger control for acquisitions of targets that received at least EUR 200,000 in a single competitive public funding event within the ten years preceding the acquisition, with a de minimis exception for transactions valued below EUR 1 million. The competition authority then has a limited period to decide whether it requires a full notification.

This approach is a well-suited trigger because a positive public funding decision presupposes an ex ante expert assessment in a competitive selection process screening for innovativeness and scaling potential: precisely the qualities that attract incumbents. A streamlined notification and a tiered procedure ensure proportionality. While it will not capture every problematic acquisition, the mechanism brings likely relevant sub-threshold acquisitions to the attention of competition authorities without creating legal uncertainty for all other sub-threshold transactions.

The proposal and its underlying ideas were developed by the author, who reviewed and edited all content and takes full responsibility.

detail.abstract: A castle, a villa on a lake, an apartment in a famous building. The listing speaks of luxury, and the asking price takes it for granted. Buyers and lenders have no yardstick for checking how much of that price is substance and how much is story. Sellers know, and the buyer pays for this asymmetry. The paper describes an independent check, carried out on public sources, that separates three things: what no one can redo; what can be redone, such as quality finishes and systems; and what the listing asserts without proof. From this comes a value range with three segments: the value of similar properties in the area, the value of replicable quality, and the share the market attributes to what is irreproducible. detail.abstract: We examine how transparency of officials' personal financial interests affects municipal borrowing costs. detail.abstract: Property tax incidence-who ultimately bears the tax burden-has long been central to public finance. In markets with imperfect competition, tax incidence may vary with market structure and strategic interactions, allowing landlords to absorb more or less of the tax burden than standard tax incidence theory would suggest. Exploiting a policy shock of a delayed comprehensive reassessment in Philadelphia and a unique property-level longitudinal rent dataset, this study revisits the issue of short-term tax incidence of property tax. We document that about 73 percent of tax increases were passed through to tenants in professionally managed large-scale apartments, with effects emerging approximately three quarters after the policy shock. However, we find no significant evidence of tax-induced rent increases at the broader market level, likely due to the smaller tax increases faced by most large multifamily properties and weaker cost pass-through among smaller rentals. This paper enriches the tax incidence literature by providing new evidence on the short-term tax pass-through and sheds light on the heterogeneity of landlord behavior, with implications for the optimal design of property tax systems.

detail.abstract:
Experts hold divergent views on AI and its potential impact on the labor market. Generative AI has the potential to improve workforce productivity by automating tasks, accelerating them, or reducing the skills required to perform them. As is true with any transformative technological change, there will be winners and losers. For example, automated telephone switching displaced switchboard operators but created new technical jobs in telecommunications maintenance and network management.

The rate at which AI diffuses through an economy and the effects it has on a labor market depend on factors such as industry composition, incumbent workers' skills, and the degree to which a nation’s infrastructure supports the many technical requirements of AI deployment. Despite the technological frontier being pushed forward almost exclusively in the United States and China, Israel and Singapore have seen the greatest level of AI utilization per capita. This suggests that AI innovators are not necessarily located in labor markets most ready to deploy and use generative solutions. This report outlines a framework for describing occupations in the context of AI, discusses labor conditions for large-scale AI adoption, proposes mitigation strategies that governments might implement to protect disaffected workers, and poses a series of open research questions that may be valuable to industry leaders and policymakers.

detail.abstract: Public pay is set by law in nominal terms, so inflation erodes its real value between legal acts until the government revises it. I model each revision as the choice of a forward-looking government, shaped by two costs that push in opposite directions. A fixed cost of acting makes revisions large and rare, whereas a convex cost of financing the increase at once makes them small and frequent. Through the budget, each revision also moves debt and the risk of fiscal stress under which the next one is made. In the documented pay decisions of eleven countries, pay set at discretion erodes against prices and private earnings and is restored in discrete steps, every cut was decided during market stress or an adjustment program, and court rulings drove a wedge between the cuts legislated, the cuts paid and the cuts that lasted. Estimated on the legal acts, the model reproduces the documented paths of pay in most countries when data and simulations are measured the same way. In Portugal's estimated model, the savings that the Treasury requires once spreads rise produce the cuts, the debt overhang holds pay down after the crisis, and a court that strikes cuts after they take effect invites cuts it will strike. Review of cuts before they took effect would have lowered the social cost of Portugal's crisis relative to review after the fact, and partial indexation would have paid in Bangladesh unless its automatic increases were costly to finance.

detail.abstract: We investigate the intraday price pressure patterns of mutual fund flows. Consistent with the demand to track Net Asset Values (NAV) priced at market close, daily fund flows are associated with abnormal returns in the net portfolio of stocks from equity funds at the US stock market's closing auction. However, 97% of the flow driven abnormal daily stock returns occur during prior market hours, with 74% occurring before the final half hour of market operations. These pre-execution stock and NAV returns partially revert over the next several trading days and impose significant execution costs in trading mutual fund shares. We calculate an implicit annual cost of roughly half a basis point on the $13.7 trillion domestic equity mutual fund portfolio for investors, adding up to $0.8 billion dollars per annum.

detail.abstract: Brazil's federal secondary schools kept in-person classes suspended longer than state and private schools during the COVID-19 pandemic but gave their students far more support for remote learning. We ask how federal students fared relative to students in the other networks, using ENEM results for the cohorts that completed secondary school from 2017 to 2025, School Census enrollment and INEP's survey of the pandemic response. Because the ENEM is voluntary, we measure participation against Census enrollment and compare equal shares of each network's enrolled cohort with changes-in-changes, a scale-free estimator. Participation fell by 26% in the federal network in 2020, against 39% in the state network. Without accounting for participation, federal students appear to lose ground relative to state students in every test, but the size of this decline depends on the score scale. Comparing equal shares of each cohort, in our main specification we find no evidence of a relative federal decline in Mathematics, Social Sciences, and Languages and Codes in the cohorts most affected by remote teaching, and relative losses in Natural Sciences and the Essay that are smaller than without the correction but statistically significant. These estimates are sensitive to assumptions on selection into the exam, to the enrollment denominators, to how students without an identified school are assigned and to prepandemic trends. The results show that conclusions about pandemic learning drawn from voluntary exams can change with the treatment of participation, the score scale and the estimator.

detail.abstract: Cross-sectional designs are widely used to estimate dynamic partial-equilibrium effects of an aggregate treatment. We show analytically that these estimates are biased when exposures to the treatment and to aggregate confounders are correlated or the confounders feed back into the treatment. This paper develops the heterogeneous-exposure local-projection instrumental variables (HELP-IV) framework, which compares units while holding the confounder path fixed by instrumenting the treatment and this path with exposure-weighted shock proxies. We prove that HELP-IV identifies the partial-equilibrium effect. We further extend the framework, with the corresponding inference, to multiple exposure margins and confounders, forward-looking outcomes, and cumulative multipliers. Finally, we apply HELP-IV to state fiscal multipliers and regional stock-wealth effects, where it yields partial-equilibrium effects that are smaller than conventional estimates and deliver different implications when ported to macroeconomic models.

detail.abstract: This study examines the extent to which risk factor disclosures convey information about shared economic exposures across firms, and whether this information varies over time or with characteristics taken to indicate boilerplate disclosure. Recent studies assert that risk factor disclosure is becoming less useful due to excessive length, stickiness, standardization, and a lack of specificity, and the SEC has expressed support for shorter disclosure. We measure risk factor disclosure similarity across firms, finding that risk factor disclosures convey at least as much information about shared economic exposures as any other individual 10-K section. The association is driven primarily by risk factor items commonly disclosed among industry peers, the language most often criticized as generic. Cross-sectional analyses suggest that the informativeness of the disclosure is stronger for longer, more standardized, and less specific disclosures. Overall, the evidence is consistent with risk factor disclosures becoming increasingly informative over time. These findings do not imply that boilerplate is useful. Rather, they indicate that the textual markers commonly used to identify boilerplate (length, stickiness, standardization, and low specificity) do not identify disclosure that is less informative about shared economic exposures.

detail.abstract: Large language models act only through the infrastructure that surrounds them. That infrastructure, the harness, determines what a model can accomplish and how it fails, yet it has no settled definition. To address this gap, we decompose the harness into eight functional components that can be specified and compared across systems, and we propose a portable specification framework that records which model ran in which harness. The record is needed because different harness configurations can yield several-fold differences in reported scores for the same model, and because much of an agent's attack surface lies in its harness. Existing model cards and agent cards provide release and operational information, but do not establish the sequence of effective configurations within a run. Harnesses can change between releases and between runs, and, where agents edit their own tools and configuration, within a run. Enacted AI laws contain documentation duties relevant to covered systems, subject to their respective scopes and application dates, but do not prescribe the common harness record proposed here. Therefore, the harness has to be explicitly described and specified as a versioned part of the system.

detail.abstract: What shapes how individuals view foreign governments and citizens, and when do these evaluations differ? We define the government-citizen evaluation gap as the direction and extent to which an observer rates the two differently, and argue that perceptions of popular control shape it. Three studies of Americans show that regime and institutional information affect government evaluations more than citizen evaluations. A pre-registered vignette experiment generates a larger pro-citizen gap under non-democracy, and a survey of real-world countries finds that the gap narrows as electoral democracy increases. Another pre-registered experiment shows that information about limited popular control widens the pro-citizen gap, primarily by lowering government evaluations, and raises relative support for government-directed punishment. A bare regime label has no detectable average effect on the gap. Openended explanations show respondents invoking citizens' limited control when distinguishing them from rulers. These findings link domestic institutions to foreign attitudes and preferences over foreign-policy targeting.

detail.abstract: This report investigates risk of refinancing concentration within the UK commercial real-estate sector, concentrating on how concentration of asset class, maturity concentration, institutional reliance, as well as interest-rate exposure affect refinancing resilience. As financing markets turn progressively interlinked, firms encounter intensified vulnerability when debt obligations, sources of funding, or maturities of loan turn clustered within specific sectors, timeframes, or institutions. The analysis assesses how these risks can influence financial stability, long-term access to capital, and liquidity management. The research adopts a relative case-study method using Landsec and SEGRO, two of the UK's biggest listed real-estate firms. The study evaluates their refinancing blueprints, diversification of funding, debt maturity frameworks, liquidity buffers, as well as hedging practices. Special focus is given to the impacts of UK macroeconomic conditions, fluctuating credit-market environments on refinancing capacity, including valuation-oriented leverage cycles. A relative evaluation of Landsec and SEGRO exhibits that both firms sustain robust refinancing resilience through diversified funding frameworks, management of active debt, debt laddering, concentration liquidity buffer, and interest-rate hedging. Nevertheless, SERGO shows a slightly robust refinancing profile owing to its long-term debt structure, wider funding diversification, more robust liquidity coverage, a well as lesser risk of maturity concentration, while Landsec gains from higher asset diversification; however, remains comparatively more exposed to office and changes in retail valuation. In aggregate, both companies are well positioned to endure overcome/endure refinancing pressures, despite SEGRO demonstrates a marginal advantage in flexibility of long-term refinancing, liquidity resilience, including safeguard against future refinancing shocks.

detail.abstract: In this post, we discuss insights from a recent staff report on the role of banking supervision in identifying and disciplining failing banks. We show that bank failures typically result from supervisory closure decisions based on hard information about book equity. Yet hard information is itself partly produced by supervision, as our evidence suggests that supervisors require troubled banks to recognize potential losses. We argue that supervision faces a tradeoff: Stricter supervision can reduce the costs of resolving failing banks, but it can also lead to tighter regulatory capital constraints and hold back credit supply.

detail.abstract: Disruptions to major transit trade corridors can substantially transform local economies by inducing population displacement, reallocating employment away from international trade, and relocating transit activities toward alternative routes. However, the direction and magnitude of these effects depend on pre-existing local economic structures and the degree of regional integration. This study analyzes these dynamics by exploiting the shock generated by the sudden closure of the Benin-Niger border following the 2023 coup d' 'etat in Niger, which cut landlocked Niger off from its primary maritime route. Employing a difference-indifferences design and using nighttime light intensity as a proxy for local economic activity, the study estimates the causal effect of the corridor disruption on economic activity in corridor-dependent localities. The findings indicate that the disruption of the Benin-Niger corridor led to a decline in economic activity in affected localities, while activity increased along the Togo-Burkina Faso-Niger corridor as traffic was redirected to this alternative route. Country-specific estimates further show that these effects are statistically significant only along the Niger and Burkina Faso segments, suggesting that the economic consequences of the closure were concentrated in the landlocked transit subregion. The results are robust to an alternative estimator, indicating that the main findings are not driven by the choice of estimation strategy.

detail.abstract: Motivated by the SEC's 2026 proposal to rescind its investment adviser pay-to-play rule, we examine whether campaign contributions distort the allocation of U.S. public pension capital to private equity (PE) managers and whether contribution restrictions mitigate these distortions. Using hand-collected data on 160 public pension plans' external managers over 2000-2022, we find that managers contributing to state politicians are 3.3 percentage points more likely to manage public pension assets in that state the following year. This association is concentrated in contributions to state officials who can influence pension investments, and is weaker for plans with separate investment boards. Triple-differences estimates indicate that the gap in the association between high-and low-corruption states narrows by approximately 80% following the SEC's 2010 pay-to-play rule. Higher contributions from PE firms also weaken the positive effects of investment delegation to external managers. Using the staggered adoption of state pay-to-play laws, we find that laws banning contributions by government contractors are followed by an estimated 84% decline in reported PE contributions and higher pension returns. Together, these findings suggest that contribution restrictions may mitigate politically distorted public pension capital allocation.

detail.abstract: Does the slope of the Phillips curve depend on how firmly inflation expectations are anchored? I examine this question using an interacted vector autoregression in which inflation dynamics vary with survey-based measures of expectations anchoring. Drawing on microdata from the Survey of Professional Forecasters and the University of Michigan, I estimate the model for the United States over 1968Q4-2026Q1. I find that the cumulative inflation response to an identified demand shock is approximately three times larger when expectations are unanchored than when they are anchored. The difference reflects stronger shock transmission rather than larger demand shocks in the unanchored regime. Regional U.S. evidence also shows a steeper inflation-unemployment relationship where household expectations are less anchored, while estimates for Brazil and the euro area support the broader pattern. A historical counterfactual suggests that the same shocks experienced during 2021-23 would have raised peak core inflation to approximately 10%, rather than the observed 6.4%, under 1970s-level anchoring. The findings highlight the role of expectations anchoring in shaping inflation dynamics and the transmission of macroeconomic shocks.

detail.abstract:
This appendix proposes two new EU own resources on intra-EU flights: a uniform VAT additive to national rates, and an ad valorem tax on vacant seats. Both are collected by the departure state and remitted in full to the EU. Confining the instruments to intra-EU flights is deliberate: it respects the norm against unilateral extraterritorial taxation with revenue retention, avoiding a repeat of the opposition to the 2012 full-scope EU ETS extension and preserving a norm that could underpin stable international financing of global public goods via future tax coalition mechanisms with earmarking obligations.

The vacant-seat tax applies a single statutory rate to the spoilage value of a departure: empty seats counted by cabin, valued at published route- and cabin-specific reference fares drawn from the previous year's realised fares. The flight-level data already exist to an audited standard, leaving fare reporting as the only genuinely new requirement.

The economic case rests on a spoilage distortion. Around 16% of EU seat-kilometres depart empty, closer to 20% weighted by revenue given higher premium-cabin vacancy, and Dörpinghaus et al. (2026) show that market outcomes systematically over-produce vacancy relative to the social optimum, with a vacant-seat tax capable of aligning airline incentives with welfare in the simplest model. There is a social welfare relevant tradeoff between carrying the same passengers with fewer aircraft and raising the risk of early sell-outs that exclude high-valuation travelers, but airlines incentives point towards over-prioritizing keeping seats for high paying late customers.

We present results for an efficiency-maximizing passenger-flow-preserving reform: it sets the vacant-seat tax to reach the efficient vacancy rate, then adjust the additive VAT so passenger numbers are unchanged. Because flows are fixed by construction, the reform places no burden on the tourism sectors. Calibration gives a vacant-seat tax of 82.6% of spoilage value and a 3.7% additive VAT, cutting vacancy from 20.1% to 2.7% and flight frequency by 17.7%. Unusually for a tax reform, it raises EUR 2.5 billion while generating surplus rather than burden: EUR 2.8 billion in partial equilibrium, plus EUR 1.8 billion once resources released from aviation flow to sectors carrying pre-existing taxes and markups, with a further EUR 0.3 billion in oil terms-of-trade gains and EUR 0.5 billion in avoided climate damages accruing to the EU.

Having established that the efficiency-maximizing passenger-flow-preserving reform should be in the interest of all EU countries, we consider a further additional reform that would raise the VAT rate beyond the modest 3.7% implied by that reform. Standard economic theory implies an optimal tax of 28 % against an 8% status quo, hence roughly a 20% additive EU VAT.

Finally, the EUR39 billion base is assigned across member states and compared to GNI shares. Malta, Greece, Cyprus, Portugal and Spain are heavily over-exposed, Germany, Slovenia and Slovakia under-exposed. The wide spread implies a standalone VAT increase would likely need compensation, motivating the suggestion to bundle it with the passenger-flow-preserving reform, whose net burden is negative.

detail.abstract: Poverty lines bundle two choices: which goods count as needs, and how much of each a household requires. The second choice is where most discretion hides. This paper shows that, when needs are satiable, it can be read from household expenditure data. We define a household's threshold as the cost of satiating the needs in a chosen basket, and show that, under stated assumptions, the cdf of thresholds equals one minus the slope of mean basket spending with respect to an independently measured budget. The conditional variance of spending gives a second marker of the lowest threshold. The line that minimizes expected misclassification cost is a quantile of the threshold distribution, and nesting results price the omission of a need. We extend the results to leakage and upgrading, give partial-identification bounds when thresholds depend on the budget, and discuss estimation by shape-constrained regression. The paper is theoretical. It does not measure the depth of deprivation or identify which individual households are poor.

detail.abstract: We develop a domain theory for the Skorokhod space D T = D([0, T ], R) with the J 1 topology that runs from abstract representation to certified numerical expectations. (i) For any complete separable metric space we construct, from finite consistent systems of rational formal balls, a bounded-complete, ω-continuous dcpo E into which the space embeds homeomorphically as the explicit G δ set n U n of ideals containing arbitrarily small balls. For D T with Billingsley's complete metric d • the primitive information objects are space-time trajectory tubes. Every classical path is maximal, and a maximal ideal is classical exactly when its closed satisfier sets have a common point. For Skorokhod space the inclusion s(D T) ⊆ Max(E) is strict, and the classical completions of a basis element are exactly its closed tube. (ii) We reduce d • on step paths to a finite-dimensional problem and prove that d • is computable on rational step paths; the model is effectively presented. (iii) Borel laws embed injectively into the probabilistic power domain, with an explicit Scott-open support test, in a framework that covers both an abstract Polish-space model and the explicit one. (iv) We define a Skorokhod-Edalat integral by lower and upper sums over simple valuations and give a self-contained proof, based on a finite splitting lemma, that every lower sum lies below and every upper sum above E µ [F ], and that the two meet when F is bounded and µa.e. J 1-continuous. The converse fails for sums over valuations below (rather than way-below) the law. (v) For jump processes we prove an exact J 1-tube probability formula for Poisson paths, an occupation-time enclosure on tubes, a positive uniformisation theorem for finitestate Feynman-Kac functionals, and a finite-state-projection bracket that turns truncated computations into rigorous bounds for countable state spaces. A reference implementation computes d • exactly, performs adaptive tube quadrature, and evaluates uniformisation bounds with outward rounding in extended precision. Applications cover quantum photon counting, a machine-certified occupation-time transform for the bistable Schlögl chemical master equation on its full state space, a closed-form arithmetic-average option under Poisson jumps, and a barrier/Asian benchmark under Merton jump diffusion. Every number reported is produced by the accompanying code, and every load-bearing claim is classified in a verification audit.

detail.abstract: Digital money on permissionless blockchains differs from previous forms of money because it unbundles trust. Instead of relying on a trustworthy institution to settle payments, it relies on decentralized verification whose cost is priced separately through congestion-sensitive gas fees. We show that these forces generate strategic complementarities in redemption decisions and can create runs even when digital money is backed by perfectly safe reserves.

detail.abstract: Performance measurement in new product development (NPD) makes realized development outcomes visible but often provides only limited insight into which stages of the development process most severely constrain performance. Yet, identifying where the causes of project failure originate is critical for firms seeking to initiate targeted process-improvement efforts and increase the likelihood of development success. To address this challenge, we develop a diagnostic framework that enables firms to uncover the unobserved performance characteristics of individual NPD stages and assess how those stages shape final development outcomes. To this end, we first characterize the information required for process identification and then devise a portfolio of practical diagnostic strategies through which firms can obtain the data needed for NPD diagnosis. For each strategy, we establish the conditions under which the underlying process characteristics can be identified and consistently estimated. Because the diagnostic strategies differ in their informational requirements, implementation complexity, operational costs, and statistical assumptions, we also discuss the settings in which each is most applicable. Ultimately, our diagnostic framework enables firms to move beyond merely measuring realized performance toward effectively diagnosing whether poor NPD performance originates in project ideation, evaluation, selection, execution, or a combination of these stages.

detail.abstract: The rapid expansion of high-speed rail (HSR) has reshaped intercity passenger transport through both substitution and complementarity. Existing studies mainly examine competition between airlines and HSR operators on overlapping corridors or cooperation in which rail acts as a feeder to major airports. This study identifies and defines a new competition problem, termed HSR-enabled indirect airline entry, in which an airline without access to slots at a congested primary airport enters a lucrative air market indirectly by flying to a nearby secondary airport and connecting passengers onward by HSR. We develop a sequential game with two airlines and three cities. Before HSR entry, Airline 1 monopolizes a lucrative trunk market to a slot-constrained primary city, while Airline 2 monopolizes a nearby secondary-city market. After the secondary and primary cities are connected by HSR, Airline 2 may enter the trunk market through an air-rail product. The incumbent provides direct air service, whereas the entrant provides a vertically differentiated transfer service. Airline 1 is capacity constrained by scarce airport slots, while Airline 2 is comparatively unconstrained at the secondary airport. Solving the game by backward induction yields three equilibrium regimes: blockaded entry, strategic deterrence, and accommodation. Under blockaded entry, the incumbent's monopoly output is already sufficient to prevent entry. Under strategic deterrence, the incumbent expands output to make entry unprofitable. Under accommodation, the entrant launches the air-rail service and both airlines coexist. The deterrence threshold increases with air-rail attractiveness, the size of the entrant's original market, and spillover intensity, but decreases with fixed entry cost. The welfare analysis shows that actual entry can reduce aggregate consumer surplus when gains from the new service and network spillovers fail to offset the withdrawal of deterrence-induced incumbent supply. Social welfare additionally accounts for the real setup cost. Within each equilibrium regime, improving the air-rail product raises consumer surplus and social welfare under strategic deterrence; under accommodation, it raises consumer surplus but may reduce social welfare. Private equilibrium choices do not always select the higher-welfare outcome. Two subsidy schemes address these differences: entry-contingent support for Airline 2 can strengthen potential competition without actual payment, whereas output-contingent support for Airline 1 can restore welfareimproving deterrence where accommodation is privately preferred. These findings distinguish the value of potential competition from that of realized entry and show why policy appraisal must consider network effects, the incumbent's response, and the design of subsidy conditions.

detail.abstract: Disability employment rose sharply in Australia after the onset of COVID-19 in 2020. While work from home (WFH) has been proposed as a key mechanism, other explanations include tight labour markets and compositional changes in the disability population. To assess these explanations, the paper combines two empirical approaches: occupation-level instrumental variable analysis, and individual-level difference-indifference models. The results suggest that expanded WFH access had, at most, a marginal effect on disability employment growth in Australia. Although correlated, increased occupational WFH has no statistically significant causal effect on disability employment once endogeneity controls are included. Instead, disability employment growth is closely linked to broader occupation-level employment growth, consistent with a tight labour market. At the individual level, people with disability had strong post-pandemic employment growth, especially those with more persistent or severe disability or receiving the Disability Support Pension. But these gains were concentrated among individuals in occupations with low pre-pandemic WFH capability, with no effect from occupation-switching after the pandemic. Overall, the findings suggest that full employment, rather than expanded access to WFH, is more important for improving disability employment outcomes, while also highlighting potential roles for institutional settings and social norms.

detail.abstract: This paper introduces a novel dataset of French administrative court decisions on urban planning and construction permits, built using Artificial Intelligence tools, including Natural Language Processing (NLP). We use this dataset to examine how the gender composition of judicial panels affects decision outcomes, and how this effect varies by applicant type. We find that panels with at least one woman significantly reduce the odds of rejecting permit-related claims-by up to 60% in some cases. Legal entities benefit more than individual applicants, especially when adjudicated by all-female panels. The gender of the presiding judge, however, does not significantly impact outcomes. These findings highlight how gender diversity influences judicial behavior, particularly through interactions with applicant identity and case complexity. By linking gender, institutional structure, and public decision-making, this study contributes new empirical insights on fairness and equity in administrative justice.

detail.abstract: Can air pollution lead to legal action? This paper investigates how French administrative courts address environmental references in construction permit litigation. Drawing on a unique dataset of 989 decisions, enriched through Natural Language Processing (NLP) techniques, we examine the social and territorial factors that shape the use of environmental references and their influence on judicial outcomes. We uncover a paradox: higher air pollution levels are associated with lower rates of environmental legal mobilization, suggesting that litigation is structurally deterred in the most polluted areas. Yet, when environmental references are supported by multiple legal references, courts are significantly more likely to favor claimants. These findings highlight selective access to environmental justice and raise critical questions about the courts' capacity to internalize environmental externalities.

detail.abstract: This study constructs measures of greenhouse gas emissions disclosure quality in SEC 10-K filings along three dimensions. Coverage captures how much a filing says about emissions. Specificity captures whether a reported quantity is attributed to Scope 1. Accuracy captures how far a Scope 1 figure falls from facility-level emissions reported to the EPA's Greenhouse Gas Reporting Program (GHGRP). Using 4,520 firm-years for 588 US firms from 2010 to 2023, this study finds that voluntary disclosure is thin: 18.7 percent of firm-year filings say nothing about emissions, 65.7 percent acknowledge the issue without a firm-specific number, and only 5.4 percent report an absolute quantity. Most Scope 1 figures that can be checked against the GHGRP understate the benchmark. Firms with emissions concentrated in a few facilities or sales concentrated in a few segments disclose less, while larger and more capital-intensive firms disclose more. Ownership share in facilities is associated with whether a firm discloses at all and, among verifiable figures, with the size of the understatement. Ownership share and capital intensity predict starting to disclose, ownership share and facility concentration predict reverting to no disclosure, and firm size predicts moving from qualitative to quantitative disclosure. The small Specificity and Accuracy samples limit generalization, but they also reflect how little voluntary disclosure there is.

detail.abstract: Concerns over the erosion of states' regulatory autonomy in digital trade agreements are increasingly framed in terms of 'digital sovereignty' or 'data sovereignty'. This chapter asks what precursors of digital sovereignty can be observed in digital trade law, as one of the dynamic fields of international economic law, what its building blocks are, and what challenges result from the shift towards it. It shows that the calibration of sovereignty has always been part of trade law, as the WTO exceptions, the 'cultural exception' and the early conflicts over privacy attest. The chapter then looks at the building blocks of contemporary digital sovereignty, which include calibrated data-related commitments and different policy space safeguarding mechanisms, such as carve-outs, general exceptions and security exceptions, as well as the more recently a proactive embedding of sovereignty in digital trade agreements. The chapter then turns to the resulting challenges and what lies ahead, including legal uncertainty and fragmentation, the increased securitization of digital trade, the asymmetric allocation of sovereignty also linked to the thin line between strategic autonomy and protectionism, and the formation of techno-blocs in the age of artificial intelligence.

detail.abstract: Europe's competitiveness challenge is increasingly linked to its limited ability to generate and scale high-growth firms. This paper examines how capital market development shapes firms' access to equity finance and how equity financing is associated with subsequent investment and innovation. Combining firm-level data from the European Investment Bank Investment Survey (EIBIS) with ORBIS financial statements and country-level indicators of capital market development, we analyse equity issuance across the European Union, the United Kingdom and the United States. We distinguish between two dimensions of capital market development: capital market depth and market size. Our results show that firms located in deeper and larger capital markets are significantly more likely to issue equity, with the strongest effects observed among young, high-growth and high-tech firms. Firms that issue equity subsequently exhibit higher investment rates, greater innovation intensity and stronger intangible investment. Simulation exercises suggest that aligning EU capital markets with deeper and more integrated benchmarks could substantially expand firms' access to equity finance. Overall, the results indicate that both the depth and scale of capital markets matter for financing firms with the greatest growth potential, thereby supporting policy efforts to deepen and integrate European capital markets.

detail.abstract: I critique André Lara Resende's September 2026 proposal to reduce Brazilian interest rates through administrative guidance and reserve intervention. I formulate a stochastic, infinite-horizon intertemporal government budget constraint under complete markets with composite debt indexation to inflation, floating nominal interest rates, and the exchange rate. The constraint organizes the paper's four analytical tasks: i) a comparison of New Classical Monetarism (NCM), the Fiscal Theory of the Price Level (FTPL), and Modern Monetary Theory (MMT); ii) a reinterpretation of the Real Plan's fiscal anchor; iii) a formalization of Brazil's post-1994 stock-flow trap; and iv) an evaluation of the Lara Resende proposal. The central result is that a unilateral cut in contractual coupons on existing bonds is a restructuring event, not a monetary easing. With a large Selic-indexed share and a large inflation-linked share, administrative rate suppression weakens the price-level shock absorber, raises risk premia, and shifts adjustment toward inflation, exchange-rate depreciation, or explicit default. Under the FTPL the proposal moves Brazil toward the feasibility boundary where no positive price level clears the valuation equation. The supporting arguments fail on their own terms: the 7.5% Selic target is arbitrary, the 4% of GDP saving estimate holds the risk premium constant, the National Fiscal and Monetary Council either duplicates or subverts Central Bank independence, and the reserve intervention strategy treats a finite external buffer as infinite. Sustainable disinflation requires stock reform and flow reform. The Turkish experiment of 2018-2023 provides the empirical analogue.

detail.abstract: The recursive budgeting estimator of [11] applies to continuous-necessity economies: its identification and asymptotic normality results (Theorems 8.1 and 8.5 of that paper) do not require discrete support (Remark 8.6 of that paper). The companion paper discusses a finite-M approximation in its Appendix F but does not develop it, citing perfect-separation concerns. This paper develops that finite-M approach for continuous-necessity economies, where phi_N takes values in a continuum (so gamma_min = 0), in the four-tier convention N, H, T, M of the companion papers. We embed the finite-M estimator in a non-standard universe and prove that, for every standard tolerance eta > 0, the finite-M approximation is exact on the set of pairs whose necessity indices are separated by at least eta. We introduce eta-separated pair approximations and show that the probability mass of the eta-diagonal band is O(eta), so the approximation is uniform off a set of arbitrarily small measure. Using Loeb measures, we show that as the sample size tends to an infinite hyperreal, the empirical distribution converges to a Loeb measure and the internal estimator is S-continuous at the population maximiser. We prove consistency of the joint M-estimator under Assumption 5.8 and a uniform Glivenko-Cantelli assumption. The transfer to the multi-stage estimator of Algorithm 1 is stated as Assumption 5.3 and is not verified in this paper. We provide a practical algorithm with a bounded choice of the finite approximation parameter M, a bootstrap-based inference procedure, and diagnostics. We illustrate the framework with a Monte Carlo simulation derived from a reduced-form three-tier consumer DGP calibrated to the recursive budgeting structure. The asymptotic distribution in the continuous case, and a proof of Assumption 5.3 under misspecification, remain open problems.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the analytical and operational foundations of inflationforecast targeting in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Using monthly data for January 2012-October 2026 and 247 sequential price reports for 2022-2026, it combines Bayesian VAR forecasting, CHAI-based inflation surveillance, local-projection transmission diagnostics and calibrated policy simulations in which price stability is the sole objective. Over forecast origins from January 2024, a parsimonious bivariate BVAR reduces root mean squared forecast errors relative to an AR(2) benchmark by 7.2-17.5 per cent across horizons of one to twelve months, although performance is sensitive to the estimation window and errors are concentrated around the 2025 stabilisation episode. CHAI adds modest predictive content beyond one price report, while associations with observed policy-rate changes are imprecise and do not identify causal effects. In a central illustrative model, forecast targeting lowers inflation losses relative to reactive and simple forecast-based rules, but these gains can reverse under transmission misspecification, and a finite-model minimax formulation performs poorly despite numerical validation. The findings support strengthening the existing forecasting and policy analysis system, liquidity management and communication before any formal change of framework, and provide a reproducible basis for assessing monetary policy choices under model uncertainty.

detail.abstract: Digital trade agreements have become critical venues for regulating cross-border digital commercial transactions, including data flows. The benefits of open digital economies have however become coupled with concerns over the erosion of states’ regulatory autonomy, and this has triggered the inclusion of a variety of safeguards within these agreements. These concerns, although of different nature, are often framed in terms of ‘digital sovereignty’ or ‘data sovereignty’ – contested concepts that this chapter first unpacks, drawing on recent scholarship and state practice, before examining how they translate into the legal notion of regulatory autonomy. The chapter also shows that digital sovereignty is increasingly pursued through trade law itself – from the EU’s digital trade agreements and digital partnerships and the AfCFTA Digital Trade Protocol to the US Agreements on Reciprocal Trade. Despite the voluntary participation of the parties in digital trade agreements, scepticism persists regarding the potential trade-offs between economic integration and regulatory autonomy. This chapter undertakes a comprehensive examination of these safeguard mechanisms, which include carve-outs, transition periods, general exception clauses, the right to regulate, legitimate public policy objective exceptions and security exceptions, taking into account the most recent treaty practice, as well as treaties in the pipeline, such as the WTO Agreement on Electronic Commerce. Through these analyses, the chapter reveals the diverse approaches adopted by countries to balance the imperatives of trade liberalization with the preservation of domestic policy space. By shedding light on the divergences in the models but also the more subtle nuances, the chapter provides a deeper understanding of the evolving dynamics of digital trade governance and its implications for national regulatory autonomy, also in light of the intensifying quest for technological sovereignty in the age of artificial intelligence.

detail.abstract: The diagnostic criterion for chasing describes the gambler who, after losing, "returns another day to get even." The field's definitions and measures treat chasing primarily as financial recoupment. "Get even" is a common English term for retaliation and recoupment, which may tell us something unexpected about why gamblers chase. Dominant explanations, including the break-even effect, frustrative non-reward, craving and cognitive distortion, are blind to the counterparty, and the psychological effects of losing to a slot machine may not be the same as those of losing to a human dealer or corporate bookmaker. This paper proposes that in a subset of gamblers, a monetary loss is processed both as an aversive outcome and (partly) as a reciprocity violation by a counterparty, making a proportion of chasing retaliatory in nature. The underlying psychological and neural processes for reciprocal exchange are evolutionarily conserved, and commercial gambling generates the relevant cues, such as an identifiable counterparty, a resource transfer and an implicit expectation of return. Retaliation is rewarding within the striatum, though the evidence implicates its dorsal region rather than the ventral striatum, the part most tied to addiction. Matched reciprocal exchange ("doubling down") escalates for a measured perceptual reason, supplying a new reading of why the chasing stake is aimed at parity ("breaking even") or at slightly overshooting it ("getting even"). This construct has been mislabeled or misconstrued, named once in 1999 but dropped by 2002, recorded as "undertones of fairness" inside the gambler's fallacy, and reported as blame directed at the gambling industry, yet filed as a failure of self-forgiveness. A few findings run against the hypothesis, as does a rival view, where persistence after a loss requires no counterparty. Discriminating tests include a scripted dealer whose apology after the same losses is sincere, sarcastic or absent, with a cooling-off pause that separates grievance from anger, and a counterparty-choice test offering a chaser worse odds against the party that took their money. Clinically, this hypothesis makes an unresolved grievance a therapeutic target that cognitive treatment should address, and there may be relevant repercussions in finance ("revenge trading").

detail.abstract: Does a place-based openness reform change how firms in host cities collaborate on innovation with firms in other cities? We study this question for the inter-city co-patenting of cities hosting China's Pilot Free Trade Zones (PFTZs), which combine investment liberalisation, trade facilitation and administrative reform in designated areas. Using a panel of 296 prefecture-level cities for 2009-2022, we verify the treatment against State Council documents, which corrects the coding of six cities and yields 52 treated cities in six cohorts. Heterogeneity-robust staggered difference-indifferences estimates (Callaway-Sant'Anna, not-yet-treated controls), conditional on baseline development and co-patenting, associate designation with about 19% more utility-model co-patent counts (95% CI 2% to 39%) and 14% more co-patent counts of all types (CI-1% to 31%). These outcomes are counts rather than shares of total patenting. The utility-model result is the clearest across the four patent types but does not survive a Holm adjustment across those four overall estimates. The invention estimate is small and imprecise (6%, CI-8% to 22%); design shows no effect. The positive estimates disappear without baseline covariates and are not robust to extrapolating pre-period trends. Among cities with co-patents, the conditional response is concentrated in co-patents per partner rather than in the number of partners. IP-enforcement heterogeneity is not supported, and city-level data cannot identify whether PFTZs widened or narrowed regional co-patenting disparities. The paper contributes conditional evidence on openness and intercity collaboration, and shows how strongly conventional two-way fixed-effects estimates depend on the assumed counterfactual.

detail.abstract: Is inconsistency a starting pitcher virtue? As paradoxical as this might sound, there are plausible theoretical reasons to think so. Under the Pythagorean Expectation Formula (PEF), a team's winning percentage can be estimated from the differential in total runs scored and allowed (James, 1983). But where a team concentrates a disproportionately large share of its runs allowed in a modest set of "lost cause" games, it necessarily will surrender a disproportionately smaller share across the remainder-and thus win more of them than PEF predicts. This is exactly the pattern that emerges when a starting pitcher's games are characterized by superior outings punctuated by occasional "blow ups." Based on this insight, theorists have proposed replacing starting-pitcher value estimators based only on run suppression with ones that appropriately credit starter variance, too (Brill & Wyner, 2024). This paper empirically investigates this "Variance Value Added" position. Combining empirically realistic simulations with historical data analyses and Bayesian estimation methods, it reaches a skeptical conclusion. A high level (90 th percentile) of starter variance, the analyses show, generates an exceedingly small return in modern baseball: less than 1 win per 162 games for an average team, and even less for a better-than-average one. Moreover, this benefit is almost entirely a consequence of chance fluctuations rather than any persistent pitcher trait in start-to-start variance. There is no reason, then, that a practical evaluator would treat starter variance as a basis for assessing pitchers over and above their ability to suppress opponent scoring.

detail.abstract: We derive the exact finite-sample distribution function, density and moments (when they exist) of the least squares estimator of the coefficient in a Gaussian firstorder autoregression. The intercept may be known or unknown and the initial observation fixed or stationary. With a fixed initial observation, the results cover every real coefficient, including the unit root and the explosive region. The joint characteristic function of the numerator and denominator of the estimation error follows from a bordered, rank-one-corrected tridiagonal Toeplitz determinant and a noncentral exponential factor. Five scalar primitives give this function, and all the derivatives that the inversion and moment formulas require, in closed form, at a cost independent of sample size. Chebyshev expansions resolve confluence near the unit root, accretivity settles the branch of the complex square root, and rearranged closed forms avoid cancellation in the explosive region. The same tools evaluate the local-to-unity limits of all four cases, including the Dickey-Fuller limits, and permit comparison with the closed-form explosive limit. In our benchmarks, exact p-values take milliseconds, and exact critical values and moments under a tenth of a second, at sample sizes from 100 to 1000000 .

detail.abstract: This study examines how barangay officials in the Philippines use ayuda, or material assistance, as a strategy to encourage citizen engagement in local governance. Using a descriptive qualitative approach, individual interviews were conducted with 28 barangay officials across Bukidnon province. Thematic analysis revealed three findings: (1) ayuda is an effective short-term motivator for participation, particularly in economically vulnerable communities, (2) officials are concerned about dependency and transactional forms of engagement, and (3) strategies such as attendance-based distribution, raffles, and food provision are commonly employed to sustain turnout. While these approaches increase citizen presence, they do not guarantee long-term and meaningful participation. This is one of the first studies to explore the perspectives of barangay officials, the implementers of ayuda, highlighting how they operationalize aid as a governance tool. The findings raise critical questions about sustainability and ethics in incentive-driven participation and recommend integrating civic education and participatory mechanisms beyond material rewards. These insights can inform policy design that balances immediate social protection with inclusive and empowered local governance.

detail.abstract:
Background: In England, many mental health hospital admissions are involuntary, a process permitted under the Mental Health Act. The number of such admissions has increased in recent years. Experiences of people who are detained are often poor. Two approaches to reduce detentions and improve experiences put forward by patients, carers, health care professionals and policy makers are independent advocacy and effective discharge planning. These both currently exist but their expansion would require resources and so it is important to consider the economic impact of doing this.

Aims: We aim to assess the impact on healthcare costs of expanding the provision of independent mental health advocacy and discharge planning

Method: Decision models were constructed to simulate the impact on costs of increasing the provision of independent advocacy for detained patients on inpatient wards and for increased provision of discharge planning both from assumed 50% baseline rates. The models incorporated the likelihood of being readmitted following the initial admission. Sensitivity analyses were conducted around key parameters to see their impact on cost savings/increases through increased provision.

Results: If coverage of advocacy increases from 50% to 55% then there are expected cost savings of £325 per person detained. If discharge planning rates are increased from 50% to 55% then there are £119 cost savings. The models were most sensitive to the impact on length of initial time in hospital, readmission length, and the likelihood of those without discharge plans being readmitted.

Conclusions: Increasing coverage of advocacy and discharge planning even by a modest amount would result in cost savings. As long as patient outcomes were not harmed, such increases represent good value for money.

detail.abstract: Plant-level instance segmentation is a key perception capability for precision agriculture, and existing public benchmarks predominantly represent specific crop sets and agricultural regions. Complementary datasets from additional crops and geographic contexts are therefore important for evaluating the generality of segmentation methods. This paper introduces FieldCrop-SWE v1.0, a Swedish farm-field RGB dataset and reproducible benchmark for crop-specific instance segmentation of cabbage, purple kale, and yellow onion. The dataset contains 620 images-241 cabbage, 155 purple kale, and 224 yellow onionwith heterogeneous image resolutions, viewpoints, and real-field conditions. Relative to representative resources such as CWFID, CropAndWeed, and PhenoBench, FieldCrop-SWE contributes a different crop combination together with a Swedish/Nordic agricultural context. Each crop is treated as an independent singleclass instance-segmentation task, reflecting field-level applications in which crop identity is known a priori and allowing plant morphology and instance density to be studied without multi-class imbalance. Four fully automatic models-YOLO12s-Seg, Mask R-CNN, YOLO26s-Seg, and Mask2Former-are evaluated using the same COCO/pycocotools mask protocol. Mask2Former records the highest AP for cabbage, purple kale, and yellow onion (65.70%, 38.16%, and 21.56%), corresponding to a mean AP of 41.81%. YOLO26s-Seg records the highest end-to-end pipeline throughput, reaching 24.89, 9.05, and 6.60 FPS on the three crop splits. All models exhibit the same difficulty ordering of cabbage > purple kale > yellow onion. The results establish an accuracy-efficiency baseline for these Swedish crops and suggest that morphology, instance density, and boundary ambiguity are important contributors to segmentation difficulty. The FieldCrop-SWE v1.0 dataset, source code, experiment notebooks, and model configurations associated with this study will be made openly available to support reproducibility and further research.

detail.abstract: Cum-fake schemes use pre-release ADRs without underlying shares to create dividend withholding tax (DWT) refund claims. Using daily ADR data for 2008-2019 and a tripledifferences design, we document lending patterns consistent with these schemes. Before 2014, excess dividend-window ADR lending equaled 0.35% of issuer market value in DWT countries, versus 0.04% for U.K. ADRs, where dividends generally face no DWT. This gap vanished after the SEC intensified scrutiny in 2014. ADR and underlying security prices show no persistent wedge. Calibration suggests a tax revenue loss of $264-640 million.

detail.abstract: In 2020, following the entry of a close competitor, Mirena, a leading hormonal intrauterine device (IUD), received its first extension of labeled duration after two decades on the market. Over the same period, 21 jurisdictions adopted laws allowing pharmacists to prescribe hormonal contraception. These developments reduced two forms of hassle costs: the burden of obtaining contraception and the frequency of returning to a provider to maintain protection. I estimate a nested logit model of contraceptive demand using Medicaid State Drug Utilization Data from 2015-2022. Counterfactual simulations show that extending Mirena's labeled duration by one year increases annual long-acting reversible contraceptive (LARC) insertions by approximately 14 percent and overall prescription contraceptive use by 2.8 percent. Nationwide pharmacist prescribing similarly increases use of eligible short-acting methods by approximately 7 percent and overall prescription contraceptive use by 4.1 percent. These responses demonstrate that reducing hassle costs induces substitution between methods while also expanding the prescription contraceptive market. In a further counterfactual, extending LARC durations to those supported by available clinical evidence generates approximately 226,500 additional annual insertions and averts an estimated 26,000 unintended pregnancies, yielding $31.8 million in projected annual net Medicaid savings after accounting for changes in contraceptive expenditures and the implied savings from avoided deliveries.

detail.abstract:
South Korea has announced the Three Megaprojects for a Great Leap Forward for Korea, roughly KRW 1,600 trillion of large-scale investment over the next decade. The plans include doubling memory chip production capacity within five years, spreading semiconductor growth hubs nationwide (including a new chip fab in the Southwest), building 8.4 GW of artificial intelligence (AI) data centers by 2029, and setting up mass production of humanoid robots.

The main battlefields of AI face severe bottlenecks, which amplifies their strategic value: CoWoS packaging in semiconductors, transformers and other power equipment and infrastructure in AI data centers, compute capacity in AI models, and real-world data and precision drive components in physical AI.

The Three Megaprojects are Korea’s bet on staking an early, strategic claim to the core bottlenecks of the global AI ecosystem. They can be seen as a specialized full-stack strategy: rather than securing the full AI stack, as the US and China are doing, they aim to secure a strategic AI corridor running from memory and advanced packaging through computing infrastructure and manufacturing data to physical AI. The aim is to build on Korea’s lead in memory, extend its semiconductor advantage into advanced packaging capability, and from there stake an early claim to the decisive points of the AI ecosystem’s hardware.

From an industrial policy perspective, the megaprojects should grow beyond a strategic AI corridor into a national growth platform that, linked with the regional growth engines, speeds the transformation of existing flagship industries and the creation of new growth engines. Their role should be redefined as a common platform that turns Korea’s flagship industries into new, AI-based growth industries through the AI transformation of all industries and the supply of compute infrastructure. Linking the megaprojects with the regional growth engines should therefore be pursued as a core policy task in opening a next-generation growth path: megaproject investment builds and grows regional industrial ecosystems, which set in motion a division of labor among the major regions and engines that accelerate growth, and so secure the nation’s industrial competitiveness.

detail.abstract: This Essay identifies a set of feasible, effective actions that federal and state governments can take to harness private sector incentives for climate change mitigation and other types of environmental protection. The environmental agenda for the post-Trump era will doubtless include proposals that focus on using standard public governance instruments, including major new legislative, regulatory, and policy initiatives, to require or subsidize private sector emissions reductions. Even if substantial growth occurs in public support for environmental protection, however, many structural obstacles will make it difficult to adopt durable, effective government policies that yield major carbon emissions reductions and other environmental benefits. Rather than relying solely on direct regulation, pricing pollution, or subsidies, the Essay explores a complementary approach: regulatory reforms and policies that federal, state, and municipal policymakers can take to harness private sector incentives to reduce carbon emissions and address other environmental issues. These steps include regulatory and policy initiatives that increase the disclosure of climate risks to investors, use federal procurement policies to encourage the inclusion of environmental requirements in private sector supply chain contracting, reduce the risks of participation in collaborative initiatives designed to disclose or reduce emissions, and facilitate pension fund, retail consumer, and real estate market pressure for climate mitigation.

detail.abstract: Privately operated facilities now supply much of the urban court capacity on which public sport participation goals depend, yet they must recover land and operating costs from paying users. Research on hybrid organisations explains how organisations combine market and social logics, but it treats time as a way of sequencing priorities across projects or years. It has not examined organisations whose scarce asset is sold by the hour. This paper introduces the concept of temporal decoupling: the practice by which a hybrid sports facility meets its community commitments by placing them in low-value hours while keeping high-value hours for its commercial logic. The paper sets out how temporal decoupling differs from classic decoupling, selective coupling and temporal compromise, draws on resource dependence theory to develop five propositions about when it occurs, and proposes two indicators, access share and the peak access ratio, that make it measurable from booking and occupancy records. The motivating setting is Greater Jakarta, Indonesia, where private racket-sport venues have multiplied while measured participation has stalled. The paper closes with implications for research and for sport policy.

detail.abstract: This paper studies the heterogeneous effects of trade in services barriers on firm-level exports, focusing on the consequences of the UK withdrawal from the European Union and the introduction of the EU–UK Trade and Cooperation Agreement (TCA). Using detailed firm-level transaction data on UK services exports combined with sectoral measures of regulatory restrictiveness, we show that UK services exports to the EU declined significantly following both the Brexit referendum and the implementation of the TCA, with substantially larger effects after regulatory barriers were formally reintroduced. The effects are highly heterogeneous across firms, following an inverted U-shaped pattern with small and large firms more negatively affected, and are particularly pronounced for foreign-owned firms using the UK as an export platform. Crucially, we show that barriers related to foreign entry are the primary drivers of the observed decline, while other regulatory dimensions play a limited role. These findings highlight the importance of firm heterogeneity and regulatory alignment in shaping services trade outcomes.

detail.abstract: This paper investigates power laws for the firm size distribution in Brazil for the largest 1000, 500 and 100 firms. A systematic nested testing strategy is implemented and stronger evidence for a Pareto type I distribution emerges only for the extreme upper tail of the distribution (top 100 firms). The Pareto exponents for the top 100 firms display a statistically significant downward trend and a structural break in 2010. Their mean falls from approximately 1.27 in 1999–2009 to 1.05 in 2010–2024, approaching the Zipf benchmark of 1 and indicating a thicker upper tail and greater revenue concentration among superstar firms.
